intro:
Habakkuk, the eighth of The Twelve (Minor Prophets), is the prophet who argues with God. Two complaints: 1) 'Why do you make me look at injustice? Why do you tolerate wrongdoing?' (Judah's sin). 2) When God says He'll use Babylon as judgment, Habakkuk protests: 'Why are you silent while the wicked swallow up the righteous?'

God's response: 'Write the revelation... though it linger, wait for it; it will certainly come.' The righteous live by faith. Then God pronounces five 'woes' against Babylon.

Habakkuk's prayer (ch 3) is a psalm of terror and trust. He recalls God's mighty acts in Exodus, then concludes: 'Though the fig tree does not bud... yet I will rejoice in the Lord.'

The book's core tension: How can a good God use a wicked nation to punish His people? Answer: God is still sovereign, Babylon will be judged too, and faith means trusting when we don't understand.
outro:
Habakkuk's dialogue form is unique—a struggling believer's honest questions. The famous line 'the righteous will live by his faith' becomes central in Paul's theology (Romans 1:17, Galatians 3:11).

The book addresses the problem of evil from within faith: not abstract philosophy but personal crisis. Habakkuk moves from complaint to confidence, not because circumstances change, but because he sees God's character.

Chapter 3 is liturgical—possibly used in temple worship. It shows that lament and trust coexist in true faith.

Habakkuk's relevance: How to maintain faith when God's ways seem contradictory. The answer isn't explanation but relationship—'I will rejoice in the God of my salvation' even when everything fails.
